title: Stochastic Fallback Policy — Simulation Playbook
body:
Context and intent:

This is a personal playbook for experimenting with stochastic fallback policies in the request routing layer. The goal is to design and evaluate lightweight, controllable fallback behaviors that trade off latency, cost, and quality when the primary model or capacity tier is unavailable or overloaded. This doc is intentionally exploratory — notes, hypotheses, config sketches, and quick simulation recipes.

Why stochastic fallbacks?
- Deterministic fallbacks (always fall back to X) create brittle behavior: capacity hotspots, deterministic degradation patterns, and poor A/B variety for QA.
- Stochastic policies can smooth load, reduce cascades, and provide signal diversity for quality monitoring.
- We want a policy layer that is simple to express in our routing config and cheap to simulate offline.

Requirements (informal):
- Expressiveness: policy should express probability distributions conditioned on signals (latency, error rate, region, customer tier).
- Observability: every decision must be tagged with metadata for downstream analytics (policy-id, sample-weight, chosen-branch).
- Safety: guaranteed minimal quality lane for enterprise customers (e.g., <1% of requests may hit degraded model).
- Backpressure-friendly: policy should be able to lower sampling when a downstream queue grows.

High-level policy shape (DSL-ish sketch):

policy_id: stochastic-fb-v1
conditions:
  - name: high-p50-latency
    when: request.latency_estimate > 200ms
    actions:
      - fallback: model-small-quantized
        probability: 0.3
      - fallback: model-medium
        probability: 0.6
      - pass_through: true
        probability: 0.1
  - name: region-us-east-spot
    when: request.region == "us-east" and capacity.tier != reserved
    actions:
      - fallback: model-medium
        probability: 0.2
      - fallback: model-small-quantized
        probability: 0.5
      - pass_through: true
        probability: 0.3

Notes: probabilities per-condition are normalized; the evaluation engine composes conditions by precedence and merges action distributions.

API surface sketch (routing decision RPC):
- Service: RouterService
- Method: DecideRoute(DecisionRequest) -> DecisionResponse

DecisionRequest (partial fields):
{
  "request_id": "string",
  "customer_tier": "reserved|standard|free",
  "region": "us-east|eu-west|apac",
  "latency_estimate_ms": 120,
  "error_rate_window_1m": 0.02,
  "model_primary": "model-xyz-v3",
  "session_context": { "kv_size": 1024 }
}

DecisionResponse (partial):
{
  "chosen_route": "hosted/model-xyz-v3",
  "policy_id": "stochastic-fb-v1",
  "branch": "pass_through|fallback-model-medium|fallback-cold-spot",
  "probability_of_choice": 0.2,
  "decision_debug": "matched-condition:high-p50-latency; sampled:0.18"
}

Simulation plan (offline):
1) Synthesize traffic traces (1M requests) with varying latency_estimate and region skew.
2) Implement a simple sampler that executes the DSL above and records decisions.
3) For each simulated decision, compute the expected cost and simulated latency using per-model profiles (tokens/s, p50, p95, cost-per-token).
4) Aggregate metrics: %requests falling to each model, expected cost per 1k req, p95 latency tail.
5) Run counterfactuals where stochastic seeds are fixed vs varied to measure variance.

Quick simulation pseudocode (Python-like):

for req in trace:
  matched = evaluate_conditions(req)
  distro = build_distribution(matched)
  x = random.random()
  branch = sample(distro, x)
  record(req.id, branch, x)

Measurement heuristics: cost and tail latency estimation formulas
- expected_cost(request, branch) = branch.cost_per_request * request.avg_tokens
- estimated_p95 = branch.base_p95 * (1 + queue_multiplier(branch.queue_len))

Safety knobs to include in policy runtime:
- hard_denials: map of customer_tier -> minimum_pass_through_prob (e.g., reserved: 0.99)
- burn_in_max: for new models, cap fallback sampling to X% until quality checks pass
- decay_on_backpressure: if downstream queue > threshold, reduce fallback sampling to relieve cold models (they may have slower cold-starts)

Instrumenting results: decision events emitted should include the following fields (minimal):
- event_type: routing_decision
- policy_id
- branch
- sample_value (0..1)
- reason_tags (list) e.g. ["p50>200","region=us-east"]
- upstream_queue_len
- downstream_latency_estimate_ms

ASCII diagram: runtime flow (simplified)

Client --> Gateway --> Router --> [Primary Model Pool]
                          |
                          v
                      [Fallback Pool(s)]

Router responsibilities:
- evaluate policy (stats+request features)
- sample branch deterministically (seed derived from request_id + policy_id for reproducibility when needed)
- tag request and emit event to telemetry pipeline

Edge cases and open questions (brain dump):
- Composition rules: how to combine multiple matching conditions? Precedence vs multiplicative composition? I prefer precedence tiers: high-safety conditions (enterprise) win first; else merge distributions by weighted average.
- Reproducibility: sometimes we want deterministic replay (for debugging A/B quality). Add a 'deterministic' flag in DecideRoute to force sampling by hashed seed.
- Audit logs: enterprise contracts may require a per-request log of fallback decisions retained for 90 days. Storage cost implications.
- Cold start dynamics: fallback often uses smaller models that might be cheaper but more brittle. Consider cooldown windows so we don't route too many requests to a freshly-woken instance.
- Explainability: downstream product teams will ask why a request saw degraded output. Make 'reason_tags' mandatory.

Small experiment ideas (order):
- E1: Static baseline: deterministic fallback to model-medium when latency_estimate>200ms. Measure tail and cost.
- E2: Stochastic policy with p=0.3 fallback to small, 0.6 fallback to medium, 0.1 pass-through. Run same trace and compare variance.
- E3: Add queue-aware decay: if model-small queue > 50, halve its sampling. Confirm decreased tail but increased cost due to pass-through.
- E4: Deterministic replay mode for top 1% of anomalies: when anomaly detected, re-run decisions with deterministic seed to reproduce path.

Checklist for moving from playbook to a tiny prototype:
- [ ] formalize DSL->JSON schema (small, no Turing-complete expressions)
- [ ] implement offline evaluator in py (10-200 lines)
- [ ] add telemetry event schema to infratelemetry repo
- [ ] run E1..E3 against synthetic traces and collect cost/latency tables
- [ ] write a 1-pager with recommended default for hosted vs dedicated customers

Final notes / thoughts:
- Keep the runtime policy simple — complexity in offline tooling and simulation is OK, runtime should be cheap to evaluate.
- Prefer explicit 'safety overrides' for enterprise contracts.
- Use deterministic-seed sampling for reproducible debug sessions, but default to non-deterministic to get smoothing benefits.

References and heuristics used in simulations:
- per-model profile table (toy):
  model-small-quantized: cost_per_request=0.0008, base_p95=220ms, throughput=1500 tok/s
  model-medium: cost_per_request=0.0025, base_p95=120ms, throughput=3000 tok/s
  model-primary: cost_per_request=0.007, base_p95=80ms, throughput=8000 tok/s

Appendix: minimal JSON policy example (for runtime ingestion)
{
  "policy_id": "stochastic-fb-v1",
  "precedence": ["enterprise-safety","latency-conditions","region-heuristics"],
  "rules": [
    {
      "id": "enterprise-safety",
      "when": {"customer_tier": "reserved"},
      "actions": [{"pass_through": true, "probability": 1.0}]
    },
    {
      "id": "latency-high",
      "when": {"latency_estimate_ms": ">200"},
      "actions": [
        {"branch": "fallback-small", "probability": 0.3},
        {"branch": "fallback-medium", "probability": 0.6},
        {"branch": "pass_through", "probability": 0.1}
      ]
    }
  ]
}

(End of playbook)
